subject: Can I use the coeffecient of variance of a posterier distribution as a metric of acuracy ?

messages.author: a997b66afa263bd1
messages.subject: Can I use the coeffecient of variance of a posterier distribution as a metric of acuracy ?
parts:
Hi Stan users

I am trying to find a single metric by which to report the expected accuracy of an estimate generated by a hierarchial regression model on STAN.  Does it make sense to use the coeffecient of variance of a posterier distribution as a metric of acuracy ? (The idea being that if the posterior is a wide normal curve with lots of variance then it's not a very ...ermm...'confident' estimate?)
I'm sorry if this is a stupid question

Thanks

messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can I use the coeffecient of variance of a posterier distribution as a metric of acuracy ?
parts:
Do you mean the coefficient of variation, ie standard deviation /
variance? That is used occasionally, when the parameter is restricted to
be positive (otherwise it makes little sense). Depends on the specifics
of your problem, but the mean and some quantiles are usually informative
enough.

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can I use the coeffecient of variance of a posterier distribution as a metric of acuracy ?
parts:
I think you're confusing the posterior std deviation with
MCMC std error. Have a look at the definitions and see if
that clears things up. A model has the posterior it has,
and that will be fat or narrow depending on the data.

And do you mean single metric for the whole model? As a proxy
for what? Held out log likelihood? If so, check out cross-validation
or WAIC.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can I use the coeffecient of variance of a posterier distribution as a metric of acuracy ?
parts:
Log density is the usual measure. Squared error a point
estimate is also traditional, but it's not probabilistic
(other than in the normal case, where it's proportional to
the log density).

- Bob
